newsitem.title: LIBERIA: Smiles as long-suffering Liberians vote.
newsitem.headline: Smiles as long-suffering Liberians vote.

text.p: Monrovia resident Moses Johnson looked lost as he stepped inside the bombed-out church where he had taken refuge for weeks as militia battles raged in the Liberian capital last year.
But as an official handed him a ballot paper, the middle-aged man smiled and stepped purposefully behind a cardboard screen inside the church.

He put a cross against a picture of his preferred presidential candidate. Still smiling, he dropped his ballot in a transparent box placed before hundreds of other voters lined up in front of the church.
"Today is a good day, and we pray to God that everything goes good. That there will be no more fighting," Johnson said.
Hundreds of Monrovia residents had lined up as early as 4.00 A.M. (0400 GMT) to vote in Liberia's first elections since 1985, hoping to usher in peace after seven years of civil war.
The church where Johnson voted is inside the Barclay Training Center barracks where some of the most savage battles took place during militia warfare in the city in April 1996.

The church still has no electric power. Polling officials inside worked from candlelight in the early morning. Later in the day streaks of sunlight filtered through mortar bomb holes in the roof and bounced off dusty chandeliers.
The international community which is financing the elections, has gone to pains to ensure a free, fair and transparent poll to prevent disputes starting new fighting.
Three former warlords, including Charles Taylor who launched the war, are running for president.
Precisely at 7.00 A.M. (0700 GMT) when polls opened, four polling officials watched by international monitors and West African peacekeepers stood before voters and held out four empty ballot boxes.
"Is there anything in this box," shouted one official.
"No," came the answer from the crowd.

The three other officials went through the same routine, then all four locked and sealed each empty box, reading out the seal numbers. The seals would be broken in public at the close of polls and voters counted on the spot.
Similar scenes took place at some 1,900 polling stations across Liberia, each protected by troops from the West African peacekeeping force ECOMOG.
Disputed polls have led to instability and war in African states from Nigeria to Uganda. Funding elections to ensure a level playing field is now a key foreign aid component.
More than 500 international poll monitors, including 52 from the European Community and more than 300 from the United Nations, fanned out across the country to observe polling.
Former U.S. president Jimmy Carter, leading his Carter Center observer team, toured polling stations in Monrovia.
"I have never seen so many people waiting in line so early to vote," said Carter, whose centre has monitored elections in places ranging from Haiti to Ghana.
Taylor started civil war in 1989 and came close to taking the capital in 1990 and 1992 but was blocked on each ocaasion by troops of the Nigerian-led ECOMOG peacekeeping force.

He looked relaxed as he voted at the McIntosh Elementary School in his Congo Town stronghold district of Monrovia. West African foreign ministers observing polling there greeted Taylor as he arrived with heavy security.
Fanatical suppporters cheered loudly when Taylor, accompanied by his wife and a three-year-old son and sporting a trademark cream safari suit, cast his vote.
"We are going to lead this government," a supremely confident Taylor told reporters.
Helen Johnson-sirleaf, Taylor's chief rival according to many analysts, voted at a station inside a compound used by peacekeepers to disarm guerrillas last year.
"We just want a clean sweep so that we can get started with the process of healing the wounds and rebuilding the country," she told reporters.
